title: Kit and the Whispering Peaks Adventure
markdown:
Kit lived so high in Oakhaven that the sky looked knitted from wool. His cottage was a triumph of tidiness. Spell scrolls stood in ranks: reluctant teacups, paired socks, the important and the merely fussy. The kettle knew its shelf. The slippers knew the hearth. Even the dust had been given a schedule and had, mostly, kept it. Fig, his donkey, had eyes like warm caramel and a talent for elbow-nudges that meant anything from teatime to are you quite sure that spell will not turn the chickens into marshmallows again. Kit had, once, turned the chickens briefly marshmallow-adjacent. Fig had not forgotten. Their days were as smooth as a path worn honest by habit, and Kit liked habit the way some wizards liked thunder.

A carriage clattered up the winding road, grand and dusty, a peacock among hens. Lady Elara stepped down twisting a silk handkerchief as if it contained the universe and had begun to leak. “Wizard Kit, is it? I have a letter. It must reach the Duke of Silverstream by dawn. The passes have thawed too early. The way is blocked.”

Kit smoothed his prim waistcoat. “A vital missive. Most certainly.” Inside, his mind did something less prim. The Whispering Peaks stole direction, howled like banshees, and vanished paths for sport. Kit’s magic was excellent for self-stirring tea and slippers that found their own feet. Heroic work in dangerous weather had always made his stomach flutter. What if the magic was only tidy, and tidiness was not enough?

“I shall escort you,” he declared, a touch high. “Fig and I know these mountains. A simple matter.” He heard himself lie with excellent posture. Fig blinked: another adventure I did not order. The handkerchief twisted. The carriage driver looked at the peaks as if they had personally insulted the horses. Dawn, however, was not taking questions, and Silverstream did not accept excuses written on mist.

The air sharpened. The road left the last slate roof and the last sensible chimney. Mist arrived like damp wool and muffled everything but their own footsteps. Lady Elara drew her cloak tight until only her worried eyes showed. Kit hummed a weaving charm against dampness, the one that kept laundry from sulking. It failed with the dignity of a wet sock. A pebble rolled off the path and took a long time to finish falling. Fig’s ears tracked it. Kit did not look down. This was not Oakhaven, where teacups came when called and socks agreed to be pairs.

A vast shadow, a storm cloud with opinions, fell over them. The ground rumbled. Ignis landed. His scales flashed sunset. His eyes were ancient and polite.

“Good day, travellers,” he boomed, thunder trying to be a butler. “I am Ignis. I observed your determined perambulations. Might I be of small assistance?”

Kit’s heart somersaulted without permission. “Ah. Unexpected. A brisk journey. Nothing more.”

“Brisk journeys benefit from draconic warmth. A guiding flight? A localised heatwave for leftover ice?”

Kit’s smile was a grimace in a waistcoat. “Most kind. We follow a specific path. Precise instructions. No undue haste.” He nudged Fig, who offered an apologetic snort. Ignis’s manners were perfect. His suggestions were a landslide of help. Kit’s carefully stacked competence felt one gust from spilling.

“The wind does seem spirited,” Ignis persisted, exhaling cinnamon smoke. “Allow me to clear your way with helpful enthusiasm!” A gale ripped leaves from trees that had survived worse winters.

“No, please!” Kit’s hands moved. An emerald shield sprang up. The wind hammered, howled, and gave up. “We prefer a gentler approach.” Sweat traced his temple. “Fig? Insights?”

Fig nudged Kit’s hand and nodded toward a faint track down a rocky embankment, more badger tunnel than road.

“Unconventional,” Ignis said. “My offer to levitate you remains viable.”

“Levitation? Nonsense!” A goblin no taller than Fig’s knee popped from behind a mossy boulder, jaunty cap lopsided, battered satchel across his chest. “Who needs levitation when you’ve got the Grotto Glide? Taran, at your service! Official Postmaster of mountain shortcuts, secret passages, and hidden ways.” He winked. “That dragon is all pomp. You need a real shortcut. Follow me!”

Taran flourished toward a cleft barely wide enough for a large cat. “Mind the slippery moss. Try not to tread on particularly grumpy grubs.” He vanished.

Kit hesitated. His route was dissolving into a well-meaning dragon and a bossy goblin. Lady Elara’s pale face decided it. “We must go,” she whispered.

“Fig,” Kit said, strained, “our straightforward journey has chosen a winding detour.” To Ignis, crestfallen on his cliff: “Meet us on the other side? We shall be remarkably swift.” Ignis inclined his magnificent head, confused and agreeable.

The Grotto Glide was a tight squeeze. Kit crawled. Fine robes snagged on rock and moss that seemed personally offended by embroidery. Water ticked somewhere in the dark, a clock with no face. Fig shuffled behind, a solid quiet, his breath warm on Kit’s heels. The air tasted of wet stone and old roots. Something small and grumpy objected to a hoof and then thought better of it. Far above, Ignis’s muffled roars attempted cinnamon assistance, a helpful thunderstorm trying to post a letter through a keyhole.

Kit pictured headlines: Wizard Trapped in Pebble Pocket. Panic arrived, cold and sharp, and clung like damp. He put one palm on Fig’s neck and counted the donkey’s breaths until his own agreed to match. The letter in Elara’s cloak rustled. Dawn, still, was not taking questions. They crawled on. A seam of pale fungus lit a bend. Taran’s jaunty cap flashed ahead like a rumour that knew the way.

They pushed out into a hidden valley under a watery sun. Taran perched on a rock with a map that appeared to be woven from living moss. “Nearly there! A short scramble to the Old Watchtower. Quickest way to Silverstream.”

“The Old Watchtower?” Kit’s voice had gone hoarse. “A perilous climb. And Ignis may offer another helping hand if he spots us.” Lady Elara’s hands were clasped white. The letter would not wait. The direct route was a stage for dragons.

“Ignis!” Kit called, surprising himself with firmness. “A small favour. Escort Lady Elara to the base of the Old Watchtower. I shall follow with Fig and keep the path clear.” Handing her over felt like setting down a duty he had promised to carry. It was also the only way to be both swift and unsinged.

Ignis, pleased to have a task, lowered his head. “Utmost expediency. A remarkable degree of gentility!”

Kit watched the dragon nudge Lady Elara onto his back. Worry arrived. Relief arrived immediately after and refused to queue. He turned to Fig. “Come, old friend. The long way. The proper way.”

They trotted a less dramatic path, the sort that switchbacked because someone long ago had respected gravity. Crisp air. Hooves on stone. A hawk. Meltwater in a ditch talked to itself. Kit talked to Fig not about wards but about the delightful absurdity of a dragon who meant well and could not grasp that one does not melt a mountain pass into submission. He described, for Fig’s benefit, the precise difference between a heatwave and a shortcut, and Fig’s ears awarded the lecture half a twitch.

Ravens crossed a sky the colour of cold iron. Kit set his palm on a boulder, sulphur and cinnamon still in the air, and let the doubt sit without answering it. Had he done the right thing, handing a letter and a lady to a creature who cleared roads with enthusiasm? Fig’s ears flicked. They went on. The watchtower’s silhouette arrived in pieces: a tooth of stone, a broken stair, a window that had forgotten glass. Kit’s waistcoat, once prim, had collected grotto souvenirs. He left them. They had been earned.

They reached the watchtower as rose and gold found the east. The last stretch was stairs that had lost arguments with frost. Fig took them like a clerk taking steps he had counted before. Lady Elara was already there, windswept, hair disobedient, safe, the letter still inside her cloak and not inside a dragon. Ignis hovered, pleased, having followed Kit’s precise if unusual instructions to the letter, which for a dragon was a kind of spell. No trees singed. No avalanche invented for courtesy. A single cinnamon puff drifted off and became morning. Taran, true to post, was already gone, hunting the next cleft, leaving only a thread of moss-map on the stair that the wind took as postage.

“Wizard Kit!” Lady Elara’s relief was genuine, the handkerchief at last unemployed. “You made it. Ignis was… enthusiastic. He brought me perfectly. The Duke will have his dawn, and I will have a story I shall edit for politeness.”

Kit bowed, small and real. It was not the rush of a grand spell. It was the steadier thing: a stack of small decisions that had held. Fig nudged his hand.

Later, in the cottage, Kit restored his scrolls to their ranks, though one grotto stain refused to be ranked and he let it stay, a small unofficial medal. The kettle found its own stir. Fig accepted a pile of hay as if hay were a treaty. When a second knock came that afternoon—a shepherd with a sock that had declared independence—Kit did not flutter. He put the sock in the pairing basket, poured tea, and asked Fig whether marshmallows were off the menu. Fig’s caramel eyes said they had always been off the menu. Outside, the peaks kept their mist and their banshee winds and their vanishing paths. Kit left the waistcoat unbuttoned one extra button, which, for him, was as good as a parade. The letter, he trusted, was already boring a Duke at breakfast.
characters: Kit (tidy wizard of Oakhaven), Fig (caramel-eyed donkey), Taran (goblin postmaster who knows all the best shortcuts)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, highland fantasy adventure for teens
